docs.text: Welcome to ARMxtend's documentation! ARMxtend (association rule mining extensions) is a Python library for mining association rules, covering the crisp and fuzzy cases, on a single machine as well as on Apache Spark for Big Data and streaming scenarios, plus meta-association rules for summarizing rules found across multiple datasets. Links Documentation: http://cjferba.github.io/armxtend Source code repository: https://github.com/cjferba/armxtend Features Crisp Fuzzy (alpha-cuts) Single machine ARM.association_rules , FFIM.fpgrowth FIM.FARE , FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth Big Data (Spark) FIM.apriori (DApriori/DAprioriTID), FIM.Eclat.DECLAT , FIM.BD_ARE FIM.BD_FARE.FuzzyDAprioriTID , FIM.Eclat.FuzzyDECLAT Streaming (Spark) SFIM (FIMoTS) + SARE.extractAssociationRules - Meta-rules (rules about rules, across multiple datasets) ARM.meta_rules.crisp_meta_association_rules ARM.meta_rules.fuzzy_meta_association_rules Plus preprocessing.FuzzyLib for fuzzifying numeric attributes and VizARM.AREtoGraph for transforming rules into the VizARE typed item/rule graph (JGF/GraphML/DOT). See the Quick Start for runnable examples of every one of these, and the User Guide for the full reference of each module. docs.text: How to Contribute I would be very happy about any kind of contribution that helps to improve and extend the functionality of ARMxtend. Getting started If you don't have a GitHub account yet, please create one to contribute to this project. Please open an issue on the issue tracker to discuss the fix or new feature before spending too much time and effort on the implementation. Fork the ARMxtend repository from the GitHub web interface, then clone your fork: git clone https://github.com/<your_username>/ARMxtend.git cd ARMxtend Install the library in editable mode (see Installation for the spark extra): pip install -e ".[spark,dev]" # pyspark + pytest, pytest-cov, ruff, mypy, build, twine, mkdocs... The tests that run on a real local Spark need a JDK 17 or 21 (set JAVA_HOME ; on macOS brew install openjdk@21 ); without one they are skipped automatically. Making changes Create a new branch for your change: git checkout -b my-feature . Implement your change, following the style of the surrounding code. Add or update unit tests under tests/ covering it. Tests for the Spark-based algorithms ( FIM.apriori , FIM.Eclat , FIM.BD_ARE , FIM.BD_FARE , SARE , SFIM ) should run against tests/spark_stub.py so they don't require a JVM/cluster. Run the same checks as the CI and make sure everything passes: ruff check . # unused/undefined names, syntax errors mypy # type check (the public API is typed; the package ships py.typed) pytest --cov=ARMxtend # tests + coverage (the CI requires >= 80 %) pytest alone runs everything ( testpaths is set in pyproject.toml ). Without pyspark the Spark-related tests are skipped, which is also how the CI checks that the core works without it. If your change affects the public API or adds a new module, update the relevant page under docs/sources/user_guide/ and add it to docs/mkdocs.yml 's nav , then check it renders correctly: cd docs mkdocs serve # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 Commit your changes with a descriptive message and open a pull request against cjferba/ARMxtend . Building and publishing the documentation From the docs directory: mkdocs build --strict # builds the static site into docs/site/, failing on broken links mkdocs gh-deploy # builds and publishes docs/site/ to the gh-pages branch Releasing a new version Releases are published to PyPI by .github/workflows/release.yml using PyPI trusted publishing (OpenID Connect): no API token is stored in the repository or the CI. One-time setup (needs the maintainer's PyPI account): On https://pypi.org/manage/account/publishing/ add a pending publisher for the project ARMxtend : owner cjferba , repository ARMxtend , workflow release.yml , environment pypi . Optionally do the same on https://test.pypi.org with environment testpypi , to rehearse a release (Actions -> Release -> Run workflow publishes the current commit to TestPyPI). In the repository settings create the environments pypi and testpypi (a required reviewer on pypi adds a manual approval before anything is uploaded). For each release: Update __version__ in ARMxtend/__init__.py and move the entries of CHANGELOG.md from unreleased to the new version. Commit, then create a GitHub release whose tag is v<version> (e.g. v0.1.0 ). The workflow refuses to publish if the tag does not match __version__ . The workflow builds the sdist and the wheel, runs twine check --strict and uploads them. Locally, python -m build && twine check --strict dist/* does the same build and check without uploading.

docs.text: Examples Every example on this page lives as a runnable, self-contained script under examples/ in the repository, and is executed on every push by tests/test_examples.py as part of the CI workflow (see the badge on the project README ). This means the code and the output shown below are guaranteed to stay in sync with the current version of the library -- if a change to ARMxtend breaks one of these examples, CI turns red. Run any of them locally with: pip install -e . python examples/example_association_rules.py Crisp association rules ( ARM.association_rules + FFIM.fpgrowth ) Mines frequent itemsets with FP-Growth and then crisp association rules (support/confidence/lift), on the classic 10-transaction, 4-item dataset used throughout the FIM papers cited in Citing ARMxtend . import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.ARM.association_rules import association_rules from ARMxtend.FFIM import fpgrowth from ARMxtend.FIM._shared import key_to_itemset TRANSACTIONS = [ "A,B,C", "B,D", "A,C,D", "B,C", "A,C", "B,D", "A,B,C", "B,C,D", "A,B,D", "B,C,D", ] def main(): transactions = [line.split(",") for line in TRANSACTIONS] freqItemsets = fpgrowth(transactions, min_supp=0.3) print("Itemsets frecuentes (min_supp=0.3):") for itemsetKey, support in sorted(freqItemsets.items()): print(" {:<10} support={:.2f}".format(itemsetKey, support)) itemsetsDf = pd.DataFrame({ "support": list(freqItemsets.values()), "itemsets": [key_to_itemset(key) for key in freqItemsets], }) rulesDf = association_rules(itemsetsDf, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.7) print("\nReglas de asociacion (min_confidence=0.7):") for _, rule in rulesDf.iterrows(): antecedent = ",".join(sorted(rule["antecedents"])) consequent = ",".join(sorted(rule["consequents"])) print(" {} -> {:<6} support={:.2f} confidence={:.2f} lift={:.2f}".format( antecedent, consequent, rule["support"], rule["confidence"], rule["lift"])) return freqItemsets, rulesDf if __name__ == "__main__": main() (full source: examples/example_association_rules.py ) Output: Itemsets frecuentes (min_supp=0.3): A support=0.50 A-B support=0.30 A-C support=0.40 B support=0.80 B-C support=0.50 B-D support=0.50 C support=0.70 C-D support=0.30 D support=0.60 Reglas de asociacion (min_confidence=0.7): A -> C support=0.40 confidence=0.80 lift=1.14 D -> B support=0.50 confidence=0.83 lift=1.04 C -> B support=0.50 confidence=0.71 {i1,i3} -> {i4} : FSupp = 0.266, FConf = 0.5, FCF = 0.33. docs.text: Every example on this page lives as a runnable, self-contained script under examples/ in the repository, and is executed on every push by tests/test_examples.py as part of the CI workflow (see the badge on the project README ). docs.text: Mines frequent itemsets with FP-Growth and then crisp association rules (support/confidence/lift), on the classic 10-transaction, 4-item dataset used throughout the FIM papers cited in Citing ARMxtend . import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.ARM.association_rules import association_rules from ARMxtend.FFIM import fpgrowth from ARMxtend.FIM._shared import key_to_itemset TRANSACTIONS = [ "A,B,C", "B,D", "A,C,D", "B,C", "A,C", "B,D", "A,B,C", "B,C,D", "A,B,D", "B,C,D", ] def main(): transactions = [line.split(",") for line in TRANSACTIONS] freqItemsets = fpgrowth(transactions, min_supp=0.3) print("Itemsets frecuentes (min_supp=0.3):") for itemsetKey, support in sorted(freqItemsets.items()): print(" {:<10} support={:.2f}".format(itemsetKey, support)) itemsetsDf = pd.DataFrame({ "support": list(freqItemsets.values()), "itemsets": [key_to_itemset(key) for key in freqItemsets], }) rulesDf = association_rules(itemsetsDf, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.7) print("\nReglas de asociacion (min_confidence=0.7):") for _, rule in rulesDf.iterrows(): antecedent = ",".join(sorted(rule["antecedents"])) consequent = ",".join(sorted(rule["consequents"])) print(" {} -> {:<6} support={:.2f} confidence={:.2f} lift={:.2f}".format( antecedent, consequent, rule["support"], rule["confidence"], rule["lift"])) return freqItemsets, rulesDf if __name__ == "__main__": main() (full source: examples/example_association_rules.py ) Output: Itemsets frecuentes (min_supp=0.3): A support=0.50 A-B support=0.30 A-C support=0.40 B support=0.80 B-C support=0.50 B-D support=0.50 C support=0.70 C-D support=0.30 D support=0.60 Reglas de asociacion (min_confidence=0.7): A -> C support=0.40 confidence=0.80 lift=1.14 D -> B support=0.50 confidence=0.83 lift=1.04 C -> B support=0.50 confidence=0.71 lift=0.89

docs.text: Installing ARMxtend ARMxtend is being prepared for its first release on PyPI (see the changelog ). Until it is published, install it from the GitHub repository : pip install git+https://github.com/cjferba/ARMxtend.git # or, to work on it, from a local checkout: git clone https://github.com/cjferba/ARMxtend.git cd ARMxtend pip install -e . Once published, pip install armxtend will be enough. It requires Python 3.9 or newer (tested on 3.9-3.12). The installation also provides the armxtend command . This installs the core, single-machine part of the library: ARM (crisp association rules and meta-rules), FIM.FARE (fuzzy association rules), FFIM (crisp and fuzzy FP-Growth), VizARM and preprocessing . Its only dependencies are numpy , pandas and networkx . Big Data / streaming extra The Big Data and streaming algorithms ( FIM.apriori , FIM.Eclat , FIM.BD_ARE , FIM.BD_FARE , SARE , SFIM ) run on Apache Spark and additionally require pyspark . Install it with the spark extra: pip install -e ".[spark]" pyspark itself requires a Java runtime (JDK 17 or 21 for PySpark 4) to be installed and on your PATH ; see the PySpark installation guide if pyspark fails to start a SparkContext . Running the tests pip install -e ".[spark,dev]" pytest The tests that run the algorithms on a real local Spark (including the FIMoTS streaming driver) need a JDK; they are skipped when none is found. The tests covering the Spark-based algorithms run against tests/spark_stub.py , a local double of the small part of the Spark RDD/broadcast API these algorithms use, so they exercise the exact same production code without requiring a real cluster or a JVM.

docs.text: Quick Start All the snippets on this page are runnable as-is (they are also covered by the test suite under tests/ ). See Installation first. 1. Crisp association rules ARM.association_rules takes a pandas.DataFrame of frequent itemsets (columns support and itemsets , as produced by FFIM.fpgrowth -- see below) and returns the rules whose metric reaches min_threshold . Besides the usual confidence / lift / leverage / conviction , it also supports certainty_factor (Shortliffe & Buchanan's CF), which unlike confidence takes the base rate of the consequent into account and is bounded in [-1, 1] : import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.ARM import association_rules df = pd.DataFrame({ "support": [0.5, 0.8, 0.7, 0.3], "itemsets": [frozenset(["bread"]), frozenset(["milk"]), frozenset(["butter"]), frozenset(["bread", "milk"])], }) rules = association_rules(df, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.5) print(rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "certainty_factor"]]) # antecedents consequents support confidence certainty_factor # 0 (bread) (milk) 0.3 0.6 -0.25 Note the negative certainty factor: although "bread -> milk" clears the 0.5 confidence bar, milk is already present in 80% of transactions on its own, so bread's presence actually decreases the belief in milk relative to its base rate -- a case confidence alone does not reveal. 2. Frequent itemsets with FP-Growth FFIM.fpgrowth mines frequent itemsets directly from raw transactions (no candidate generation), returning a dict {itemset_key: support} ready to feed into association_rules after converting it to the expected DataFrame shape ( FIM._shared.key_to_itemset undoes the 'A-B-C' key encoding): from ARMxtend.FFIM import fpgrowth from ARMxtend.FIM._shared import key_to_itemset from ARMxtend.ARM import association_rules import pandas as pd transactions = [ ["bread", "milk"], ["bread", "diapers", "beer", "eggs"], ["milk", "diapers", "beer", "cola"], ["bread", "milk", "diapers", "beer"], ["bread", "milk", "diapers", "cola"], ] freq_itemsets = fpgrowth(transactions, min_supp=0.5) df = pd.DataFrame({"support": list(freq_itemsets.values()), "itemsets": [key_to_itemset(k) for k in freq_itemsets]}) rules = association_rules(df, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.7) 3. Fuzzy association rules Fuzzy itemsets and rules generalize the crisp case to items with a degree of membership in [0, 1] (e.g. "cold" or "low humidity" instead of a hard threshold). FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth mines fuzzy frequent itemsets by decomposing the fuzzy database into num_alpha alpha-cuts (10 is a good default, see Fernandez-Basso, Ruiz & Martin-Bautista, 2021 ); FIM.FARE.fuzzy_association_rules then derives the fuzzy support (FSupp), confidence (FConf) and certainty factor (FCF), integrating the crisp measure at each alpha-cut weighted by the width of that cut (see the FARE user guide for the exact formulas): from ARMxtend.FFIM import fuzzy_fpgrowth from ARMxtend.FIM.FARE import fuzzy_association_rules # each transaction: a list of (item, membership degree in [0, 1]) pairs fuzzy_transactions = [ [("cold", 1.0), ("low_humidity", 0.8)], [("cold", 0.9), ("low_humidity", 0.6)], [("warm", 0.7), ("low_humidity", 0.9)], [("cold", 0.6), ("low_humidity", 0.7)], [("warm", 1.0), ("low_humidity", 0.2)], ] freq_itemsets = fuzzy_fpgrowth(fuzzy_transactions, min_supp=0.3, num_alpha=10) rules = fuzzy_association_rules(freq_itemsets, num_alpha=10, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.5) print(rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "certainty_factor"]]) FIM.Eclat.FuzzyDECLAT and FIM.BD_FARE.FuzzyDAprioriTID mine the same kind of fuzzy frequent itemsets, but distributed on Spark (see section 5 below). 4. Meta-association rules When you have already mined association rules independently from several datasets (e.g. one per store, sensor, or time period), ARM.meta_rules finds "rules about rules": which primary rules tend to co-occur across a high enough proportion of the datasets, optionally together with extra attributes of each dataset. This is useful both to summarize a large number of per-dataset rules and to spot cross-dataset patterns invisible in any single dataset (see Ruiz et al., 2016 ). from ARMxtend.ARM.meta_rules import mine_primary_rule_measures, crisp_meta_association_rules, \ fuzzy_meta_association_rules store1 = [["bread", "milk"]] * 6 + [["bread"]] * 2 + [["milk"]] * 2 store2 = [["bread", "milk"]] * 5 + [["bread"]] * 3 + [["milk"]] * 2 store3 = [["cola", "chips"]] * 7 + [["cola"]] * 3 # Step 1: mine primary crisp rules (and their confidence) independently per dataset rule_measures = mine_primary_rule_measures([store1, store2, store3], min_supp=0.3, min_conf=0.5) # -> [{'milk=>bread': 0.75, 'bread=>milk': 0.75}, {'milk=>bread': 0.71, 'bread=>milk': 0.62}, {'chips=>cola': 1.0, 'cola=>chips': 0.7}] # Step 2a: crisp meta-rules -- only presence/absence of each primary rule matters crisp_meta = crisp_meta_association_rules([set(m) for m in rule_measures], min_supp=0.5, min_conf=0.9) print(crisp_meta[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence"]]) # bread=>milk <-> milk=>bread, support=0.67 (found in 2/3 datasets); chips<->cola rules are # dropped, since they were only found in 1/3 datasets (below min_supp) # Step 2b: fuzzy meta-rules -- also weighs how strong (confident) each primary rule was fuzzy_meta = fuzzy_meta_association_rules(rule_measures, num_alpha=10, min_supp=0.3, min_conf=0.5) print(fuzzy_meta[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence"]]) 5. Big Data (Spark) FIM.apriori , FIM.Eclat and FIM.BD_ARE / FIM.BD_FARE mirror the algorithms above but distribute the counting across a Spark cluster ( pip install -e ".[spark]" , see Installation ). They take a pyspark.SparkContext and an RDD of transactions instead of a plain Python list: from pyspark import SparkContext, SparkConf from ARMxtend.FIM.apriori import DApriori from ARMxtend.FIM.BD_ARE import association_rules_bd sc = SparkContext(conf=SparkConf().setAppName("armxtend-quickstart").setMaster("local[*]")) transactions = sc.parallelize([ "bread,milk", "bread,diapers,beer,eggs", "milk,diapers,beer,cola", "bread,milk,diapers,beer", "bread,milk,diapers,cola", ]) freq_itemsets = DApriori.run(sc, transactions, min_supp=0.5) # or DAprioriTID, or Eclat.DECLAT rules = association_rules_bd(sc, freq_itemsets, min_conf=0.7) SFIM mines frequent itemsets over a Spark Streaming sliding window (see SFIM.main ), and SARE.extractAssociationRules extracts association rules from its current frequent-itemset tree. 6. Visualizing rules VizARM.AREtoGraph turns a rules DataFrame into the VizARE typed graph -- item nodes and rule nodes connected by antecedent / consequent edges, following Fernandez-Basso et al. (2026, see Citing ARMxtend ) -- ready to export to JSON Graph Format, GraphML, or DOT (Gephi, Cytoscape, Graphviz, NetworkX): from ARMxtend.VizARM import AREtoGraph graph = AREtoGraph.from_dataframe(rules, rule_measures=("confidence", "certainty_factor")) jgf = graph.exportGraph(type=0) # 0: JGF, 1: GraphML, 2: DOT, 3: the networkx.DiGraph itself graph.to_html("rules.html") # interactive, self-contained viewer: open it in any browser 7. Fuzzifying numeric attributes preprocessing.FuzzyLib turns a numeric column into a set of overlapping fuzzy labels (a triangular Ruspini partition), ready to be used as items in the fuzzy pipelines above: import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.preprocessing import FuzzyLib fuzzy_lib = FuzzyLib() fuzzy_lib.data = pd.DataFrame({"temperature": [15, 19, 22, 25, 28]}) added_columns = fuzzy_lib.Fuzzification(["temperature"], [[18, 22, 26]], [["cold", "comfort", "warm"]]) # adds temperature_cold, temperature_comfort, temperature_warm columns, degrees summing to 1 per row

docs.text: FFIM -- FP-Growth (crisp and fuzzy) Single-machine frequent itemset mining via FP-Growth (Han, Pei & Yin, 2000): builds a frequent pattern tree and mines it recursively without generating candidates, which is usually faster than Apriori/Eclat-style approaches on a single machine. Crisp: fpgrowth fpgrowth(transactions, min_supp) transactions ( Sequence[Iterable[str]] ): one transaction per element. min_supp ( float ): minimum relative support, in (0, 1] . Returns dict {itemset_key: support} , e.g. {"bread": 0.8, "bread-milk": 0.6, ...} -- convert a key back to a frozenset with FIM._shared.key_to_itemset before feeding it to ARM.association_rules . from ARMxtend.FFIM import fpgrowth transactions = [ ["bread", "milk"], ["bread", "diapers", "beer", "eggs"], ["milk", "diapers", "beer", "cola"], ["bread", "milk", "diapers", "beer"], ["bread", "milk", "diapers", "cola"], ] fpgrowth(transactions, min_supp=0.5) # {'beer': 0.6, 'beer-diapers': 0.6, 'milk': 0.8, 'diapers-milk': 0.6, # 'bread-milk': 0.6, 'diapers': 0.8, 'bread-diapers': 0.6, 'bread': 0.8} Fuzzy: fuzzy_fpgrowth fuzzy_fpgrowth(transactions, min_supp, num_alpha) transactions ( Sequence[Iterable[Tuple[str, float]]] ): each transaction is a list of (item, membership degree in [0, 1]) pairs. num_alpha ( int ): number of alpha-cuts used to decompose the fuzzy database (10 is a reasonable default, see Citing ARMxtend ). Since the FP-tree merges transaction paths that share the same items, it cannot directly accommodate arbitrary real-valued membership degrees (two transactions with identical items but different degrees would stop being "the same path"). fuzzy_fpgrowth works around this by binarizing the fuzzy database independently at each of the num_alpha alpha-cuts (see FIM._shared.alpha_cuts ) to discover candidate itemsets, then recomputing each candidate's exact support at every alpha-cut. docs.text: SFIM / SARE -- streaming frequent itemsets and association rules (Spark) Requires the spark extra ( pip install -e ".[spark]" , see Installation ). FIMoTS (Frequent Itemset Mining over Time-sensitive Streams) mines frequent itemsets over a Spark Streaming sliding window, implementing the distributed algorithm of Fernandez-Basso, Francisco-Agra, Martin-Bautista & Ruiz (2019) -- see Citing ARMxtend . Rather than rescanning the whole window on every new batch of transactions, it maintains a Frequent Itemset Tree (FIT) together with per-itemset transforming bounds that bracket how many transactions can be added/removed before an itemset's frequent/infrequent status could possibly change, so only itemsets close to that boundary need their support recomputed. SFIM and SARE share the exact same FIMoTS implementation ( FIMoTS_Structure , FIMoTS_Tree , FIMoTS_Node , FIMoTS_List , FIMoTS_Bounds , WindowData , DecimalFraction , FIMoTS_Algorithm ). SARE additionally extracts association rules from the current tree of frequent itemsets -- the extension to association rule mining that the 2019 paper lists as future work. Running the algorithm from ARMxtend.SFIM import main # or ARMxtend.SARE main(minSuppNum=1, minSuppDen=3, mode="STREAMING", intervals=5, hostname="localhost", port=9999, threads=2, seconds=5) minSuppNum / minSuppDen : minimum relative support, as a fraction of integers (e.g. 1/3). mode : "TEXTFILE" for a static dataset (one transaction per line, items separated by spaces, read from filesDir ) or "STREAMING" to receive transactions in real time via Spark Streaming. intervals : number of time intervals (batches of transactions) that make up the sliding window. SARE.main additionally accepts minConf : if given, association rules with confidence >= minConf are extracted and printed after every window update, alongside the frequent itemsets. SARE.extractAssociationRules extractAssociationRules(actual_fimots_structure, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.7) Extracts crisp association rules from the frequent itemsets currently held in a FIMoTS_Structure (built and kept up to date by SARE.main / FIMoTS_Algorithm ). Because the FIT already stores, by construction, the support of every non-empty subset of each frequent itemset (candidates are generated by combining shorter frequent itemsets), extracting rules reduces exactly to the crisp, non-distributed case: this function builds the pandas.DataFrame expected by ARM.association_rules from the tree, and delegates to it. from ARMxtend.SARE import extractAssociationRules rules = extractAssociationRules(actual_fimots_structure, min_threshold=0.7) See tests/test_sare_association_rules.py for a runnable example that builds a FIMoTS_Structure by hand (without running the full streaming algorithm) and verifies the extracted rules against FIM.BD_ARE.generate_rules . Correctness verification and notes tests/test_fimots_streaming.py runs the algorithm on a real local Spark and, after every window slide, compares the frequent itemsets it maintains incrementally with a brute-force computation over the transactions currently in the window. The scenarios include concept drift (item frequencies change halfway through the stream), item names that are prefixes of each other ( milk / milkshake ), items that appear for the first time after the initial window, and several window sizes and support thresholds. Writing this check uncovered, and fixed, four defects in the incremental maintenance (a fresh initialization of the same window was always right; the incremental path was not): an itemset that became frequent was never added as a partner to its already-expanded left siblings (e.g. c_e was lost when e became frequent), so frequent itemsets went missing; items that first appear after the initial window never got a node, and so were never detected; sibling and descendant lookups matched node keys with startswith , mixing up items whose names are prefixes of other names, and pruning an infrequent itemset only removed its direct children, leaving deeper descendants behind; when two sibling itemsets became frequent in the same window, their common child was created twice, registered twice in the bounds lists and counted double. Notes: item names must not contain _ (it is the key separator of the tree) nor be -1 (the root key). SFIM now simply re-exports the implementation of SARE , so both always behave the same.

docs.text: VizARM.AREtoGraph Transforms a set of association rules into the VizARE typed graph, following: Fernandez-Basso, C., Ruiz, M.D., Molina-Solana, M., Martin-Bautista, M.J. (2026). VizARE: An Intermediate Representation to Support the Visualization of Association Rules in Data Mining . Future Internet, 18(7), 374. See Citing ARMxtend . Unlike a flat item-to-item graph (where an edge would join every antecedent item directly to every consequent item, losing the rule's structure as soon as it has more than one item per side), VizARE uses two node types -- item and rule -- connected by directed edges with an explicit semantic role: antecedent (item -> rule) and consequent (rule -> item). A rule's measures of interest (support, confidence, lift, ...) live as attributes of its own rule node , not of an edge, and a rule with several antecedent/consequent items is simply a rule node with several incoming/outgoing edges -- no ambiguity, no information lost. Building the graph AREtoGraph.from_dataframe(rules_df, rule_measures=("support", "confidence", "lift")) The most convenient entry point: builds the graph directly from a rules pandas.DataFrame , in the same format returned by ARM.association_rules or FIM.FARE.fuzzy_association_rules (columns antecedents / consequents as frozenset s of items, plus one column per measure named in rule_measures ). from ARMxtend.ARM.association_rules import association_rules from ARMxtend.VizARM import AREtoGraph rules = association_rules(freq_itemsets_df, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.5) graph = AREtoGraph.from_dataframe(rules, rule_measures=("support", "confidence", "certainty_factor")) Or build it rule by rule with add_rule(antecedent, consequent, measures) (Algorithm 1, RulesToGraph , of the paper) -- useful when the rules don't come from a DataFrame: graph = AREtoGraph() graph.add_rule(["temperature_cold", "occupation_low"], ["hvac_off"], measures={"support": 0.31, "confidence": 0.87}) Item nodes get a group attribute -- the attribute name of the item, used by the paper for indexing/visualization -- inferred by default from the attribute_value naming convention already used by preprocessing.FuzzyLib (e.g. "temperature_cold" -> group "temperature" ); pass your own item_group_fn(item) -> str to add_rule / from_dataframe to override it. Alternatively, AREtoGraph(path, MeasuresRules, MeasuresItems=None, SepRule=";", SepFI=";", SepItems=",") loads rules from a CSV file with antecedents / consequents columns (items joined by SepItems ) plus one column per measure in MeasuresRules ; load_item_measures(path) attaches per-item measures (e.g. support) from a second CSV. Rule summarization (optional) graph.summarize(signature="antecedent_consequent", measures=("support", "confidence")) Section 4.2 of the paper: when the rule set is large, inspecting one node per rule becomes cluttered. summarize adds a summary node per group of rules sharing the same signature ( "antecedent" , "consequent" , or "antecedent_consequent" , the default), aggregating each measure's min / max / mean /quantiles across the group and keeping a members list of the original rule ids for drill-down. Summary nodes connect to the same item nodes, with the same antecedent / consequent semantics as regular rule nodes, so a visualization tool can render either the full rule-level graph or the summarized one: for summaryId in graph.summarize(signature="consequent"): data = graph.graph.nodes[summaryId] print(data["rule_count"], "rules ->", data["members"]) Interactive viewer graph.to_html("rules.html", title="Smart office rules", max_rules=150, sort_by="lift", measure="lift") Writes a single, self-contained HTML file -- no CDN, no server, no network access: it opens in any browser, can be e-mailed or archived, and embeds the graph itself in the paper's JGF format ( to_jgf_dict() ), so the viewer consumes exactly the intermediate representation. What you get: automatic force-directed layout; zoom (scroll), pan (drag the background), pin a node by dragging it (double-click to release); hover tooltips and a details panel with the readable rule ( A, B -> C ) and all its measures; selecting or hovering a node highlights its neighbours and dims the rest; search (Enter centres on the first match), minimum-value slider for any rule measure, and size/colour of the rules by that measure ; switches for the item / rule / summary layers (see Rule summarization ); summary nodes list their member rules as links. Arguments: path (write the file), title , max_rules + sort_by (keep only the best max_rules rules by that measure, with their items and the summaries they belong to), measure and min_value (initial measure and threshold). The layout uses a spatial grid for repulsion, so thousands of nodes stay interactive (about 3,300 nodes / 16,000 edges ran at roughly 48 fps in our test), but a graph with that many edges is a hairball for human eyes: use max_rules , the threshold slider or the summaries to explore large rule sets. Graph and document databases The paper (Section 4.3) stores the intermediate form natively in Neo4j or MongoDB: graph.to_cypher() # CREATE (:Item {...}); CREATE (:Rule {...}); ... (:ANTECEDENT / :CONSEQUENT) relationships graph.to_documents() # {'nodes': [{'_id': ..., 'kind': ..., 'confidence': ...}], 'edges': [...]} to_cypher() returns statements ready for cypher-shell or the Neo4j browser (strings are escaped); to_documents() returns flat documents with the measures as top-level fields so they can be indexed and queried ( {"kind": "rule", "confidence": {"$gte": 0.8}} ) after collection.insert_many(...) . Both accept max_rules / sort_by . Exporting graph.exportGraph(type=0) # JGF (JSON Graph Format) -- the paper's proposed intermediate form graph.exportGraph(type=1) # GraphML string (Gephi / Cytoscape / NetworkX) graph.exportGraph(type=2) # DOT string (Graphviz) graph.exportGraph(type=3) # the underlying networkx.DiGraph JGF (also available directly as graph.to_jgf() / graph.to_jgf_dict() ) is the format proposed by the paper as an interoperability layer between rule-mining algorithms and visualization tools -- it can be stored as-is in a document database (MongoDB) or loaded into a graph database (Neo4j) for querying, and is natively understood by graph-visualization libraries such as D3.js , Bokeh , Gephi or NetworkX : graph = AREtoGraph.from_dataframe(rules) print(graph.to_jgf()) # { # "graph": { # "directed": true, # "type": "association-rules", # "nodes": { # "A": {"label": "A", "metadata": {"kind": "item", "group": "A"}}, # "rule::A=>C": {"label": "A -> C", "metadata": {"kind": "rule", "support": 0.4, "confidence": 0.8, ...}} # }, # "edges": [ # {"source": "A", "target": "rule::A=>C", "relation": "antecedent", "metadata": {}}, # {"source": "rule::A=>C", "target": "C", "relation": "consequent", "metadata": {}} # ] # } # } Write the GraphML/DOT result to a .graphml / .dot file to open it in your graph visualization tool of choice, or work with the networkx.DiGraph ( type=3 ) directly for further analysis (centrality, community detection, ...) using networkx .

docs.text: Command line: armxtend Installing the package adds the armxtend command (also available as python -m ARMxtend ). It works on a single machine, without Spark, and covers the most common one-shot tasks: armxtend rules transactions.csv --min-supp 0.1 --min-threshold 0.7 armxtend fuzzy-rules sensors.csv --labels 3 --alpha 10 --metric certainty_factor --min-threshold 0.5 armxtend gradual-rules health.csv --min-supp 0.3 --min-threshold 0.9 armxtend --version rules -- crisp association rules transactions.csv : one transaction per line, items separated by --delimiter (default , ), - reads from standard input. Mines the frequent itemsets with FP-Growth ( FFIM.fpgrowth ) and the rules with ARM.association_rules . $ armxtend rules transactions.csv --min-supp 0.3 --min-threshold 0.7 antecedents consequents support confidence lift certainty_factor D B 0.5000 0.8333 1.0417 0.1667 A C 0.4000 0.8000 1.1429 0.3333 C B 0.5000 0.7143 0.8929 -0.1071 fuzzy-rules -- fuzzy association rules from numeric columns A CSV with a header. Numeric columns (or those in --columns ) are fuzzified automatically with FuzzyLib.AutoFuzzification ( --labels , --method uniform|quantile|kmeans , --membership triangular|trapezoidal|gaussian ), mined with fuzzy_fpgrowth ( --alpha alpha-cuts) and turned into rules with FIM.FARE . --measures adds extra interest measures as columns. gradual-rules "The more A, the more B" rules directly on the numeric columns ( ARM.gradual_rules ); --max-rows works on a random sample for big tables. docs.text: Scalability of the Spark algorithms This page reports how the Big Data algorithms ( FIM.apriori.DApriori , DAprioriTID , FIM.Eclat.DECLAT , FIM.BD_FARE.FuzzyDAprioriTID , FIM.Eclat.FuzzyDECLAT ) behave on a real Spark as the data, the number of cores and the number of items grow. The measurements come from benchmarks/spark_scalability.py , which you can re-run on your own machine or cluster. What these numbers are, and are not. Everything below was measured on one machine in Spark's local[n] mode. It shows how the work is spread over cores and how the cost grows with the data. It says nothing about network cost, shuffles between nodes, or HDFS/S3 reads in a real cluster: ARMxtend has not been measured on a cluster yet. The data are synthetic and each number is the best of two runs on a machine that was doing nothing else; expect run-to-run variation of up to about 30 %. Set-up Machine Apple M2 Pro, 10 cores (6 performance + 4 efficiency), 16 GB RAM, macOS Software Python 3.12, PySpark 4.2.0, OpenJDK 21, spark.driver.memory=6g Data synthetic baskets of about 10 items drawn with Zipf-like popularity, written as 8 text files and read with sc.textFile Mining min_supp = 0.05 , 100 distinct items unless stated otherwise (about 250 frequent itemsets); fuzzy runs use 5 alpha-cuts export JAVA_HOME=... # a JDK 17 or 21 python benchmarks/spark_scalability.py all --output results.json Growth with the number of transactions (8 cores) Seconds per run: Transactions DApriori DAprioriTID DECLAT FuzzyDAprioriTID FuzzyDECLAT 25 000 0.89 1.05 0.49 1.8 3.8 50 000 1.19 1.43 0.70 3.2 9.6 100 000 1.84 2.39 1.15 6.6 20.2 200 000 3.21 3.64 1.74 - - 400 000 5.84 7.25 3.52 - - Fitting t ~ N^a gives a = 0.69 ( DApriori , DAprioriTID ), 0.70 ( DECLAT ), 0.93 ( FuzzyDAprioriTID ) and 1.20 ( FuzzyDECLAT ) . The crisp exponents are below 1 because each Spark job has a fixed cost of a few tenths of a second; the last doubling (200 000 to 400 000) multiplies the time by 1.8 to 2.0, so the crisp algorithms are linear in the number of transactions once the data are big enough to hide that fixed cost. FuzzyDAprioriTID is also close to linear. FuzzyDECLAT grows faster than the data (see below), and the fuzzy algorithms were only run up to 100 000 transactions. Speed-up with the number of cores (200 000 transactions) Seconds, with speed-up S = T1 / Tn and efficiency E = S / n : Cores DApriori DAprioriTID DECLAT FuzzyDECLAT 1 14.4 17.9 3.5 61.1 2 7.4 (S 1.95, E 98 %) 9.2 (S 1.94, E 97 %) 2.3 (S 1.53, E 77 %) 37.2 (S 1.64, E 82 %) 4 4.0 (S 3.61, E 90 %) 5.0 (S 3.57, E 89 %) 1.7 (S 2.00, E 50 %) 37.5 (S 1.63, E 41 %) 8 3.4 (S 4.20, E 52 %) 4.2 (S 4.29, E 54 %) 1.8 (S 1.97, E 25 %) 44.4 (S 1.38, E 17 %) DApriori and DAprioriTID scale almost ideally up to 4 cores. At 8 cores the efficiency drops to about 50 %: eight Python workers and the driver compete for 10 cores, four of which are slow efficiency cores, and the fixed per-job cost is now a large share of a 3-second run. Take the 8-core figure as a property of this machine. DECLAT is the fastest algorithm on one core but stops improving after 2 to 4 cores, because the TID-lists are collected and processed in the driver (see below). FuzzyDECLAT does not scale with more cores and is even slower with 8 than with 2. FuzzyDAprioriTID was not part of this experiment. Memory of the driver DECLAT and FuzzyDECLAT build the TID-lists with groupByKey().collectAsMap() , so all of them end up in the driver process , and then broadcast them. This is the algorithm's design (the DECLAT paper already notes it is the most memory-hungry), and it sets the size of the data they can handle by the memory of the driver, not by the size of the cluster. Peak resident memory of the Python driver process at 400 000 transactions, each algorithm measured in a fresh process: Algorithm Driver memory before / peak DApriori 120 MB / 121 MB DECLAT 120 MB / 402 MB (about 0.7 KB per transaction) FuzzyDECLAT needs much more because every TID carries a vector with one value per alpha-cut: the peak resident memory of the driver process was 411, 708 and 1 303 MB at 25 000, 50 000 and 100 000 transactions (roughly 12 MB per 1 000 transactions with 5 alpha-cuts; these peaks come from the general benchmark run, where the process had already executed the smaller sizes, so they are upper bounds). That vector is also shipped to every worker in a broadcast and its supports are computed with Python loops, which explains the super-linear time and the lack of speed-up. Number of items and caching of the input Distinct items (100 000 transactions, 50 to 400 items): the time decreases (for DApriori , 2.3 s with 50 items down to 1.0 s with 400). The cost is driven by the number of frequent itemsets (466 with 50 items, 108 with 400 at this min_supp ), not by the number of distinct items. Caching the input RDD ( rdd.cache() before the call): no measurable difference in local mode (for example DApriori , 1.64 s without and 1.74 s with caching). Reading a local text file is cheap, so this experiment cannot tell whether it helps when the input comes from HDFS or S3. The algorithms make several passes over the RDD, so caching a slow-to-read input is the usual Spark advice, but that benefit has not been measured here and the algorithms do not cache anything themselves. Recommendations For big crisp data use DApriori or DAprioriTID : they are linear in the data and the only ones whose speed-up was close to ideal. DECLAT is faster for moderate data, as long as all the TID-lists fit in the driver. For big fuzzy data use FuzzyDAprioriTID . Avoid FuzzyDECLAT beyond a few tens of thousands of transactions. A low min_supp multiplies the number of frequent itemsets and hence the work, much more than extra items do. Give the driver enough memory ( spark.driver.memory ) when you use the Eclat variants. For the streaming algorithm (FIMoTS) the relevant guarantee is correctness rather than speed: after every window slide its result is checked against a brute-force count on a real Spark (see SFIM / SARE ). Its throughput has not been benchmarked.

docs.text: ARM.association_rules Generates crisp association rules from a set of frequent itemsets already mined (e.g. with FFIM.fpgrowth or FIM.apriori / FIM.Eclat on Spark). Signature association_rules(df, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.8, support_only=False) df ( pandas.DataFrame ): frequent itemsets, with columns support (float) and itemsets (a frozenset of items). metric ( str ): one of "support" , "confidence" , "lift" , "leverage" , "conviction" , "certainty_factor" or any of the additional measures below. min_threshold ( float ): minimum value of metric for a rule to be returned. support_only ( bool ): if True , only computes support (useful when df does not contain the support of every antecedent/consequent needed for the other metrics). Returns a pandas.DataFrame with columns antecedents , consequents , antecedent support , consequent support , support , confidence , lift , leverage , conviction , certainty_factor , plus one column per additional measure. Additional interest measures All are functions of (supp(AB), supp(A), supp(B)) (equivalently of the 4-fold table <a, b, c, d> = <sAB, sA-sAB, sB-sAB, 1-sA-sB+sAB> ), defined in ARMxtend.ARM._measures . They are neutral ( 0 ) when undefined ( 0/0 ), never NaN . Measure ( metric= ) Definition Range Symmetric jaccard sAB / (sA + sB - sAB) [0, 1] yes cosine sAB / sqrt(sA sB) [0, 1] yes kulczynski (Conf(A->B) + Conf(B->A)) / 2 -- robust to null transactions (Wu, Chen & Han, 2010) [0, 1] yes all_confidence sAB / max(sA, sB) = min(Conf(A->B), Conf(B->A)) [0, 1] yes max_confidence max(Conf(A->B), Conf(B->A)) [0, 1] yes added_value Conf(A->B) - supp(B) (Tan, Kumar & Srivastava, 2004) [-1, 1] no zhangs_metric (sAB - sA sB) / max(sAB(1-sA), sB(sA-sAB)) (Zhang, 2000) [-1, 1] no yules_q (ad - bc) / (ad + bc) [-1, 1] yes For asymmetric-direction questions use added_value , zhangs_metric or certainty_factor ; for "are A and B just co-occurring?" the symmetric ones. In the fuzzy case ( FIM.FARE ) every one of them is evaluated at each alpha-cut and aggregated with the RL-theory weights, exactly like FConf and FCF . Certainty factor Besides the classic confidence/lift/conviction, metric="certainty_factor" computes the Shortliffe & Buchanan certainty factor (Delgado, Ruiz & Sanchez): CF(A -> B) = (Conf(A->B) - supp(B)) / (1 - supp(B)) if Conf(A->B) > supp(B) = (Conf(A->B) - supp(B)) / supp(B) if Conf(A->B) < supp(B) = 0 if Conf(A->B) = supp(B) Unlike confidence, CF is bounded in [-1, 1] and takes the base rate of the consequent into account: a positive value means the antecedent genuinely increases belief in the consequent, a negative value means it decreases it (a negative or independent association -- exactly the kind of rule that plain confidence can misleadingly rank as "interesting"), and 0 means no change. See Citing ARMxtend for the reference. Example import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.ARM import association_rules df = pd.DataFrame({ "support": [0.5, 0.8, 0.7, 0.3], "itemsets": [frozenset(["bread"]), frozenset(["milk"]), frozenset(["butter"]), frozenset(["bread", "milk"])], }) rules = association_rules(df, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.5) print(rules[["antecedents", "consequents", "support", "confidence", "certainty_factor"]]) # antecedents consequents support confidence certainty_factor # 0 (bread) (milk) 0.3 0.6 -0.25 Here confidence alone (0.6 >= 0.5) would flag "bread -> milk" as interesting, but the negative certainty factor reveals that milk is already present in 80% of all transactions, so bread's presence actually makes milk less likely relative to its base rate.

docs.text: ARM.exception_rules -- exception and anomalous rules Patterns describing when a strong rule fails . Both start from a strong "common sense" rule A -> b and relate to the treatment of absence in Section 4 of Delgado et al. (2011), based on Suzuki (1997) and Delgado, Ruiz & Sanchez (2011, Int. J. Uncertainty, Fuzziness and KBS , 19(2)). from ARMxtend.ARM import exception_rules, anomalous_rules !!! note "Formulation" The conditions below are a direct formulation in terms of support and confidence. The original papers contain more general variants (other measures, "double" rules); check them if you need those exact definitions. Exception rules For a strong rule A -> b , an exception is a set of items Z such that A ^ Z -> ~b is strong ( exception_confidence >= min_exception_conf , with the much lower min_exception_supp : exceptions are rare), and the reference rule Z -> ~b is not strong ( reference_confidence <= max_reference_conf ), so the exception is due to the combination A ^ Z and not to Z alone. exception_rules(transactions, min_supp=0.1, min_conf=0.8, min_exception_supp=0.01, min_exception_conf=0.8, max_reference_conf=0.5, max_condition_size=1, rules=None) data = ([{"fever", "rest"}] * 60 + [{"fever", "must_work"}] * 5 + [{"must_work", "rest"}] * 35 + [{"fever", "hospital"}] * 10) exception_rules(data, min_supp=0.3, min_conf=0.8, min_exception_supp=0.03) # {fever} -> rest (conf 0.80), but with {must_work}, ~rest: confidence=1.00 (reference 0.12) Returns a DataFrame with antecedents (A), consequent (b), condition (Z), common_support , common_confidence , exception_support , exception_confidence and reference_confidence , sorted by exception confidence. rules= accepts a precomputed association_rules result; otherwise the common rules are mined with min_supp / min_conf . max_condition_size allows conditions with several items. Anomalous rules For a strong rule A -> b , the anomalies are the cases where A holds but b does not ( A ^ ~b ). An anomalous rule A ^ ~b -> C says that C characterizes them ( anomalous_confidence >= min_anomalous_conf ), where A -> C is not strong ( reference_confidence <= max_reference_conf ) -- C is not already usual when A holds. anomalous_rules(transactions, min_supp=0.1, min_conf=0.8, min_anomalous_supp=0.01, min_anomalous_conf=0.8, max_reference_conf=0.5, max_anomaly_size=1, rules=None) Returns antecedents , consequent , anomaly (C), common_support , common_confidence , anomalous_cases (number of transactions with A ^ ~b ), anomalous_support , anomalous_confidence and reference_confidence . Only common rules with a single-item consequent are used: the negation of a multi-item consequent is a disjunction ( ~(b1 ^ b2) = ~b1 v ~b2 ), which Delgado et al. warn may not be of interest. Supports of A ^ Z ^ ~b are counted directly on the transactions (they are usually too rare to be recovered from a frequent-itemset result).

docs.text: ARM.gradual_rules -- gradual rules Dependencies such as "the more age and the less exercise, the higher the cholesterol" , mined directly from numeric columns -- no discretization or fuzzification. Based on Hullermeier (2002), "Association rules for expressing gradual dependencies" (PKDD 2002). import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.ARM import gradual_rules, format_gradual_itemset rules = gradual_rules(health_df, min_supp=0.25, min_conf=0.8) for _, r in rules.iterrows(): print(format_gradual_itemset(r["antecedents"]), "->", format_gradual_itemset(r["consequents"])) # age↑, exercise↓ -> cholesterol↑ support=0.51 confidence=0.98 Model A gradual item is (attribute, direction) , with direction '+' ("the more") or '-' ("the less"); a gradual itemset has items of distinct attributes. A pair of rows (s, t) satisfies an itemset if, going from s to t , every attribute moves in its indicated direction (strictly: ties do not count). Support = fraction of the n(n-1)/2 unordered row pairs that satisfy the itemset (in either orientation); confidence of A -> B = supp(A u B) / supp(A) . Support is anti-monotone, so the search is a level-wise Apriori with pruning. An itemset and its mirror (all directions flipped: "the more A, the more B" = "the less A, the less B") have the same support, so only the canonical form (first attribute '+' ) is generated; every returned rule has an equivalent mirror rule that is not listed. docs.text: ARM.meta_rules Meta-association rules: mining associations over a set of association rules already extracted from multiple datasets, following Ruiz, Gomez-Romero, Molina-Solana, Campana & Martin-Bautista (2016) -- see Citing ARMxtend . Given k datasets D_1, ..., D_k sharing a domain (e.g. one per store, sensor, or time window), each yielding a set of primary association rules R_1, ..., R_k , a meta-database is built where each row is a dataset D_j and each column (item) is a rule r_i (plus, optionally, extra attributes of the dataset). Mining association rules over this meta-database yields meta-rules such as r1 ^ r2 -> r3 (rules that co-occur across a high proportion of datasets) or r1 -> at2 (a rule associated with a dataset attribute). Two variants are provided, mirroring Algorithms 3 and 4 of the paper: Crisp ( crisp_meta_association_rules ): the meta-database is boolean -- 1 if the rule was found in that dataset, 0 otherwise. Only presence/absence matters, not how strong the rule was. Fuzzy ( fuzzy_meta_association_rules ): the meta-database uses the rule's own support or certainty factor in that dataset as its fuzzy degree, so a rule mined with confidence 0.95 contributes more than one mined with confidence 0.51 -- the resulting meta-rules incorporate the quality of the primary rules, not just their presence. !!! warning "Rule and item identifiers" Identifiers used as meta-database items (rule keys, attribute names) must not contain the - character, since it is used internally as the itemset-key separator. Use rule_key() to build safe rule identifiers. Mining the primary rules mine_primary_rule_measures(datasets, min_supp=0.1, min_conf=0.5, metric="confidence") Mines crisp rules independently in each dataset of datasets (a list of transaction lists) using FFIM.fpgrowth + ARM.association_rules , and returns one dict {rule_key: metric value} per dataset -- the input expected by both meta-rule variants below. Crisp meta-rules build_crisp_meta_database(rule_sets, attributes=None) crisp_meta_association_rules(rule_sets, attributes=None, min_supp=0.5, min_conf=0.5, metric="confidence") rule_sets ( Sequence[Set[str]] ): for each dataset, the set of rule keys found in it (or a dict , as returned by mine_primary_rule_measures -- only its keys are used). attributes ( Sequence[dict[str, int]] , optional): extra boolean attributes per dataset. Fuzzy meta-rules build_fuzzy_meta_database(rule_measure_sets, attributes=None, normalize=False) fuzzy_meta_association_rules(rule_measure_sets, attributes=None, num_alpha=10, min_supp=0.1, min_conf=0.5, metric="confidence", normalize=False) rule_measure_sets ( Sequence[dict[str, float]] ): for each dataset, {rule_key: measure in [0, 1]} -- the output of mine_primary_rule_measures . normalize ( bool ): if True , scales each rule's column to [0, 1] by its maximum across datasets (useful when every primary rule's support is very low in absolute terms). Example from ARMxtend.ARM.meta_rules import mine_primary_rule_measures, crisp_meta_association_rules, \ fuzzy_meta_association_rules store1 = [["bread", "milk"]] * 6 + [["bread"]] * 2 + [["milk"]] * 2 store2 = [["bread", "milk"]] * 5 + [["bread"]] * 3 + [["milk"]] * 2 store3 = [["cola", "chips"]] * 7 + [["cola"]] * 3 rule_measures = mine_primary_rule_measures([store1, store2, store3], min_supp=0.3, min_conf=0.5) # [{'milk=>bread': 0.75, 'bread=>milk': 0.75}, # {'milk=>bread': 0.71, 'bread=>milk': 0.62}, # {'chips=>cola': 1.0, 'cola=>chips': 0.7}] crisp_meta = crisp_meta_association_rules([set(m) for m in rule_measures], min_supp=0.5, min_conf=0.9) # bread=>milk <-> milk=>bread, support=0.67 (found in 2/3 stores); # the chips<->cola rules are dropped (found in only 1/3 stores, below min_supp) fuzzy_meta = fuzzy_meta_association_rules(rule_measures, num_alpha=10, min_supp=0.3, min_conf=0.5)

docs.text: ARM.negative_rules -- rules with absent items Rules such as A -> ~B ("if A, then not B"), ~A -> B or ~A -> ~B , where ~i means that item i is absent from the transaction. Crisp and fuzzy versions, following Section 4 of Delgado, Ruiz, Sanchez & Serrano (2011) -- see Citing ARMxtend . from ARMxtend.ARM import negative_association_rules drinks = [{"coffee", "sugar"}] * 30 + [{"tea"}] * 25 + [{"tea", "sugar"}] * 5 + [{"coffee"}] * 10 rules = negative_association_rules(drinks, min_supp=0.25, min_threshold=0.95) # {coffee} -> {~tea} support=0.57 confidence=1.00 # {tea} -> {~coffee} support=0.43 confidence=1.00 # {coffee, sugar} -> {~tea} ... How absence is modelled Absent items are added to the transactions as ordinary items named ~item and mined with the same algorithms ( FFIM.fpgrowth / FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth ), so every measure, threshold and downstream tool works unchanged. An itemset never contains both i and ~i (its support is 0), so trivial rules such as i -> ~i cannot appear. In the fuzzy case, the absence of an item is its complement at every alpha-cut level (Eqs. (27)-(28) of the paper) -- not the fuzzy-set negation 1 - degree . The 4-fold table of (~A, B) is <c, d, a, b> obtained from the one of (A, B) , so no new frequencies are needed, and FSupp(~A) = 1 - FSupp(A) holds exactly. E.g. a degree 0.6 with Lambda = {1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2} holds at the levels 0.6, 0.4, 0.2 ( FSupp = 0.6 ) and its absence at 1, 0.8 ( FSupp = 0.4 ). The explosion of absent items In sparse data the absence of an item is almost always frequent, and the number of itemsets explodes (support of absence does not satisfy the upward closure used for pruning). Two controls, both from the paper: only_frequent_positive=True (default): only items whose positive form is frequent are negated (the restriction of Han & Beheshti adopted in Section 6 of the paper). negate_items=[...] : explicitly restrict which items can appear as absent. Signatures negative_association_rules(transactions, min_supp, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.8, negate_items=None, only_frequent_positive=True, only_negative=True) fuzzy_negative_association_rules(transactions, min_supp, num_alpha, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.8, negate_items=None, only_frequent_positive=True, only_negative=True, measures=None) transactions : crisp: Sequence[Iterable[str]] ; fuzzy: a list of (item, degree) pairs per transaction, as produced by FuzzyLib.GetFuzzyTransactions . only_negative ( True ): return only rules with at least one absent item; False also returns the purely positive ones. metric / min_threshold / measures : any measure of ARM.association_rules (crisp) or FIM.FARE (fuzzy). Item names must not contain - (the itemset-key separator). Helpers: negate("A") == "~A" , is_negated("~A") , add_absent_items(transactions, negate_items=None) .

docs.text: ARM.redundancy -- pruning redundant rules from ARMxtend.ARM import prune_redundant_rules pruned = prune_redundant_rules(rules, tol=1e-9) A rule X2 -> Y2 is redundant if another rule X1 -> Y1 is more general -- smaller or equal antecedent ( X1 ⊆ X2 ) and larger or equal consequent ( Y1 ⊇ Y2 ) -- with exactly the same support and confidence (Bastide, Taouil, Pasquier, Stumme & Lakhal, 2000, Mining minimal non-redundant association rules using frequent closed itemsets ). The general rule asks for fewer conditions and concludes at least as much, so it carries all the information of the redundant one. Duplicated rules are reduced to one. On a typical rule set the reduction is large: for the 5-transaction example of examples/example_rule_types.py , 12 rules are reduced to 5. rules : any DataFrame with antecedents / consequents (frozensets), support and confidence columns: the output of ARM.association_rules , FIM.FARE , ARM.negative_rules or ARM.gradual_rules . tol : absolute tolerance to consider two support/confidence values equal (use a larger value for fuzzy rules computed from many alpha-cuts if you want to merge near-ties). support_column , confidence_column : to prune by other column names. It preserves the structure and relative order of rules .

docs.text: FIM.BD_ARE -- crisp association rule mining (Spark) Requires the spark extra ( pip install -e ".[spark]" , see Installation ). Mines crisp association rules from a set of frequent itemsets already computed (e.g. with FIM.apriori.DApriori / DAprioriTID or FIM.Eclat.DECLAT ), implementing Algorithm 4 ("Spark procedure for association rule mining") of Fernandez-Basso, Ruiz & Martin-Bautista (2024) -- see Citing ARMxtend . Rule generation is the part shared by all three frequent-itemset-mining algorithms above. generate_rules (sequential) generate_rules(freq_itemsets, min_conf) The plain-Python computation, useful for small itemset sets or for testing: for every frequent itemset, generates all its possible antecedent/consequent splits and keeps those with confidence >= min_conf . association_rules_bd (distributed) association_rules_bd(sc, freq_itemsets, min_conf) Same computation as generate_rules , distributed across the cluster via a Spark flatMap + filter over the candidate itemsets (broadcasting freq_itemsets so every partition can look up antecedent/consequent supports). Both take freq_itemsets ( dict {itemset_key: support} , as returned by DApriori / DAprioriTID / DECLAT ) and min_conf (minimum confidence, in (0, 1] ), and return dict {(antecedent_key, consequent_key): confidence} . from ARMxtend.FIM.apriori import DApriori from ARMxtend.FIM.BD_ARE import association_rules_bd freq_itemsets = DApriori.run(sc, transactions, min_supp=0.5) rules = association_rules_bd(sc, freq_itemsets, min_conf=0.7)

Fuzzy frequent itemset mining on Apache Spark, inspired by Apriori-TID, implementing Algorithm 1 ("BDFARE-Apriori"/"BDFARE-Apriori-TID") of Fernandez-Basso, Ruiz & Martin-Bautista (2021) -- see Citing ARMxtend . FuzzyDAprioriTID.run(sc, transactions, min_supp, num_alpha) sc ( pyspark.SparkContext ). transactions ( RDD[Iterable[Tuple[str, float]]] ): each transaction is a list of (item, membership degree in [0, 1]) pairs. min_supp ( float ): minimum aggregated fuzzy support (FSupp), in (0, 1] . num_alpha ( int ): number of alpha-cuts used to decompose the fuzzy database (the paper experimentally shows 10 equidistributed alpha-cuts are enough to uncover every significant fuzzy association rule). Returns dict {itemset_key: numpy.ndarray(num_alpha)} : the bit-list of relative support of each frequent itemset at every alpha-cut (see FIM._shared.alpha_cuts ) -- the same output convention as FIM.Eclat.FuzzyDECLAT and FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth , so all three are interchangeable as input to FIM.FARE.fuzzy_association_rules . from ARMxtend.FIM.BD_FARE import FuzzyDAprioriTID fuzzy_transactions = sc.parallelize([ [("cold", 1.0), ("low_humidity", 0.8)], [("cold", 0.9), ("low_humidity", 0.6)], [("warm", 0.7), ("low_humidity", 0.9)], ]) freq_itemsets = FuzzyDAprioriTID.run(sc, fuzzy_transactions, min_supp=0.3, num_alpha=10) Scalability FuzzyDAprioriTID grows almost linearly with the number of transactions (fitted t ~ N^0.93 between 25 000 and 100 000 transactions on a local Spark), which makes it the recommended fuzzy algorithm for big data; the alternative FuzzyDECLAT keeps all the membership vectors in the driver. docs.text: FIM.Eclat -- DECLAT / FuzzyDECLAT (Spark) Requires the spark extra ( pip install -e ".[spark]" , see Installation ). Frequent itemset mining on Apache Spark inspired by the sequential ECLAT algorithm (Zaki, 2000), which represents each item by its list of transaction identifiers (TID-list) and computes an itemset's support by intersecting the TID-lists of its items. DECLAT (crisp) Implements Algorithm 3 of Fernandez-Basso, Ruiz & Martin-Bautista (2024) -- see Citing ARMxtend . docs.text: FIM.FARE -- fuzzy association rules (single machine) FARE (Fuzzy Association Rule Extraction) generates association rules from fuzzy frequent itemsets, using the alpha-cut decomposition of the Representation by Levels (RL) theory of Delgado, Ruiz, Sanchez & Serrano (2011), as formalized for Big Data by Fernandez-Basso, Ruiz & Martin-Bautista (2021) -- see Citing ARMxtend . Fuzzy transactions and itemsets A fuzzy transaction t assigns every item i a membership degree t(i) in [0, 1] . An itemset A 's membership degree in t is the minimum of its items' degrees: t(A) = min_{i in A} t(i) . A crisp transaction is the special case where every degree is 0 or 1. Alpha-cuts and the FSupp / FConf / FCF measures Rather than picking a single threshold, a fuzzy measure is computed by decomposing [0, 1] into a set of p equidistant alpha-cuts Lambda = {alpha_1 > alpha_2 > ... > alpha_p} (with alpha_(p+1) = 0 by convention), and integrating the corresponding crisp measure at every cut, weighted by the cut's width (alpha_i - alpha_(i+1)) : FSupp(A) = sum_i (alpha_i - alpha_(i+1)) * |{t : t(A) >= alpha_i}| / |D| FSupp(A -> B) = sum_i (alpha_i - alpha_(i+1)) * |{t : t(A) >= alpha_i and t(B) >= alpha_i}| / |D| FConf(A -> B) = sum_i (alpha_i - alpha_(i+1)) * |{t : t(A) >= alpha_i and t(B) >= alpha_i}| / |{t : t(A) >= alpha_i}| FCF(A -> B) = sum_i (alpha_i - alpha_(i+1)) * CF_i(A, B) where CF_i is the crisp certainty factor (see ARM.association_rules ) computed from the 4-fold table at level alpha_i . Note FSupp(A -> B) = FSupp(A U B) , since t(A U B) = min(t(A), t(B)) >= alpha_i exactly when both t(A) >= alpha_i and t(B) >= alpha_i . When |{t : t(A) >= alpha_i}| = 0 at some level (the antecedent never appears at that level), that level's confidence term is taken to be 1, following the "0/0" convention in Ruiz et al. (2016). For equidistant alpha-cuts, every weight equals 1/p , so FSupp / FConf / FCF are simply the average of the crisp measure across the p alpha-cuts. fuzzy_association_rules fuzzy_association_rules(freq_itemsets, num_alpha, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.8, measures=None) freq_itemsets ( dict[str, numpy.ndarray] ): fuzzy frequent itemsets, mapping 'A-B-C' to its bit-list of relative support at each of num_alpha alpha-cuts, as returned by FIM.Eclat.FuzzyDECLAT , FIM.BD_FARE.FuzzyDAprioriTID or FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth (all three are interchangeable). Must include the bit-list of every non-empty subset of each itemset -- guaranteed by the downward-closure property of those mining algorithms. num_alpha ( int ): number of alpha-cuts used to mine freq_itemsets (must match). metric ( str ): "support" (FSupp), "confidence" (FConf), "certainty_factor" (FCF) or any other measure of ARM.association_rules except conviction (unbounded level by level): lift , leverage , jaccard , cosine , kulczynski , all_confidence , max_confidence , added_value , zhangs_metric , yules_q . Each is computed at every alpha-cut and aggregated with the weights (alpha_i - alpha_(i+1)) . min_threshold ( float ): minimum value of metric for a rule to be kept. measures ( list[str] , optional): extra measures to add as columns of the result. Returns a pandas.DataFrame with columns antecedents , consequents , support (FSupp), confidence (FConf) and certainty_factor (FCF), plus one column per entry of measures . Example Reproducing the numerical example of Ruiz et al. (2016), Section 4.4 (fuzzy database in their Table 2, itemset A={i1,i3} -> B={i4} , alpha-cuts {1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2} ): from pyspark import SparkContext from ARMxtend.FIM.Eclat import FuzzyDECLAT from ARMxtend.FIM.FARE import fuzzy_association_rules sc = SparkContext(master="local[*]") degrees = { "i1": [1, 1, 0.4, 0.6, 0.4, 0], "i2": [0.2, 1, 0.1, 0, 0.1, 1], "i3": [1, 0.8, 0.7, 0.4, 0, 0], "i4": [0.8, 0, 0.6, 0.4, 0, 0], "i5": [0.9, 0, 0, 0.5, 0, 0], } transactions = sc.parallelize([[(item, degrees[item][t]) for item in degrees] for t in range(6)]) freq_itemsets = FuzzyDECLAT.run(sc, transactions, min_supp=0.0, num_alpha=5) rules = fuzzy_association_rules(freq_itemsets, num_alpha=5, metric="support", min_threshold=0.0) rule = rules[(rules["antecedents"] == frozenset(["i1", "i3"])) & (rules["consequents"] == frozenset(["i4"]))] print(rule[["support", "confidence", "certainty_factor"]]) # support confidence certainty_factor # 0 0.266667 0.5 0.33 matching the paper's reported FSupp=0.266 , FConf=0.5 , FCF=0.33 exactly (see tests/test_fim_fare.py ).

docs.text: FIM.apriori -- DApriori / DAprioriTID (Spark) Requires the spark extra ( pip install -e ".[spark]" , see Installation ). Frequent itemset mining on Apache Spark, inspired by the sequential Apriori and Apriori-TID algorithms, implementing Algorithms 1 and 2 of Fernandez-Basso, Ruiz & Martin-Bautista (2024) -- see Citing ARMxtend . DApriori DApriori.run(sc, transactions, min_supp) sc ( pyspark.SparkContext ): used to create broadcast variables with the candidate itemsets at each iteration. transactions ( RDD[str] ): one transaction per line, items separated by , (customize via DApriori.item_sep ). min_supp ( float ): minimum relative support, in (0, 1] . Returns dict {itemset_key: support} with every frequent itemset of any length (candidates are generated with the classic apriori-gen procedure, pruning any candidate with an infrequent subset -- see FIM._shared.generate_candidates ). DAprioriTID Same signature and result as DApriori . The difference is internal: after the first pass, items are sorted by descending support and infrequent items are removed from every transaction, so later iterations scan a smaller, pre-filtered dataset -- matching the memory-usage advantage reported for Apriori-TID over plain Apriori on large datasets. Example from pyspark import SparkContext, SparkConf from ARMxtend.FIM.apriori import DApriori, DAprioriTID sc = SparkContext(conf=SparkConf().setAppName("armxtend").setMaster("local[*]")) transactions = sc.parallelize([ "bread,milk", "bread,diapers,beer,eggs", "milk,diapers,beer,cola", "bread,milk,diapers,beer", "bread,milk,diapers,cola", ]) freq_itemsets = DApriori.run(sc, transactions, min_supp=0.5) # or: DAprioriTID.run(sc, transactions, min_supp=0.5) Feed the result into FIM.BD_ARE.association_rules_bd to mine association rules.

docs.text: FIM.condensed -- closed and maximal itemsets from ARMxtend.FIM import closed_itemsets, maximal_itemsets, support_from_closed Condensed representations of a frequent-itemset result ( {'A-B-C': support} ), valid for the output of any ARMxtend miner, crisp (scalar support: FFIM.fpgrowth , FIM.apriori , FIM.Eclat , ...) or fuzzy (support = bit-list per alpha-cut: FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth , FIM.Eclat.FuzzyDECLAT , ...). closed_itemsets(freq_itemsets, tol=1e-12) -- itemsets with no proper superset of exactly the same support (Pasquier et al., 1999). They preserve the support of every frequent itemset with fewer entries. maximal_itemsets(freq_itemsets) -- itemsets with no frequent proper superset (Bayardo, 1998). Even smaller, but the supports of the subsets are lost. support_from_closed(itemset, closed) -- recovers the support of any frequent itemset as the maximum support among the closed itemsets that contain it ( None if it is not frequent). from ARMxtend.FFIM import fpgrowth baskets = [{"a", "b", "c"}] * 3 + [{"a", "b"}] + [{"d"}] frequent = fpgrowth(baskets, min_supp=0.2) # 8 itemsets closed_itemsets(frequent) # {'a-b': 0.8, 'a-b-c': 0.6, 'd': 0.2} maximal_itemsets(frequent) # {'a-b-c': 0.6, 'd': 0.2} support_from_closed("a-c", closed_itemsets(frequent)) # 0.6 In the fuzzy case, two itemsets have "the same support" only if their bit-lists coincide at every alpha-cut, i.e. closure is defined level by level, consistently with the RL-theory.

docs.text: preprocessing.FuzzyLib Loads a tabular dataset and fuzzifies its numeric attributes into named fuzzy sets (e.g. Temperature -> cold / comfort / warm ), ready to be used as fuzzy items in FIM.FARE , FIM.BD_FARE , FIM.Eclat.FuzzyDECLAT or FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth . Loading data fuzzy_lib = FuzzyLib() fuzzy_lib.LoadData("path/to/data.csv") # or set fuzzy_lib.data directly to an existing DataFrame fuzzy_lib.GetData() # the underlying pandas.DataFrame fuzzy_lib.GetAtributes() # column names fuzzy_lib.GetTypes() # column dtypes Fuzzification Fuzzification(Atri, thresholds, FuzzyLabel, membership="triangular") Atri ( list[str] ): names of the numeric attributes to fuzzify. thresholds ( list[list] ): for each attribute, the parameters of its fuzzy sets, one per label: ascending peaks ( membership="triangular" ), (a, b, c, d) vertices ( "trapezoidal" ) or (center, sigma) pairs ( "gaussian" ). FuzzyLabel ( list[list[str]] ): for each attribute, the name of each fuzzy label (same length as its thresholds entry). membership ( str ): "triangular" (default), "trapezoidal" or "gaussian" -- see below. With the default membership="triangular" , this computes a triangular Ruspini partition : given n ascending peaks p_1 < ... < p_n (one per label), the two extreme labels are "shoulders" (full membership beyond their own peak) and the intermediate ones are triangles centered on their peak, so that the membership degrees of all n labels always sum to 1 for every row. It adds one new column <attribute>_<label> per label, with its membership degree, and returns the list of added column names. import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.preprocessing import FuzzyLib fuzzy_lib = FuzzyLib() fuzzy_lib.data = pd.DataFrame({"temperature": [15, 19, 22, 25, 28]}) added_columns = fuzzy_lib.Fuzzification(["temperature"], [[18, 22, 26]], [["cold", "comfort", "warm"]]) print(fuzzy_lib.data) # temperature temperature_cold temperature_comfort temperature_warm # 0 15 1.00 0.00 0.00 # 1 19 0.75 0.25 0.00 # 2 22 0.00 1.00 0.00 # 3 25 0.00 0.25 0.75 # 4 28 0.00 0.00 1.00 Each row's fuzzified columns for that attribute sum to 1: fuzzy_lib.data[added_columns].sum(axis=1) . Trapezoidal and Gaussian sets fuzzy_lib.Fuzzification(["temperature"], [[(-float("inf"), -float("inf"), 15, 20), # cold: 1 up to 15 (15, 20, 25, 30), # comfort: core 20-25 (25, 30, float("inf"), float("inf"))]], # warm: 1 from 30 [["cold", "comfort", "warm"]], membership="trapezoidal") fuzzy_lib.Fuzzification(["temperature"], [[(15.0, 3.0), (22.0, 3.0)]], [["cold", "warm"]], membership="gaussian") # exp(-(x-center)^2 / (2 sigma^2)) A trapezoid (a, b, c, d) is 0 up to a , rises to 1 at b , stays 1 until c and falls to 0 at d ( a == b / c == d give vertical sides; -inf / +inf give shoulders). Trapezoids and Gaussians need not sum to 1 per row. The functions are also available on their own in ARMxtend.preprocessing.membership . Automatic fuzzification AutoFuzzification(Atri=None, n_labels=3, method="quantile", FuzzyLabel=None, membership="triangular") Computes each attribute's partition from its data (all numeric columns if Atri is omitted), so you do not need to choose breakpoints by hand: method Peaks "uniform" evenly spaced between the min and max "quantile" (default) evenly spaced quantiles (min, ..., median, ..., max): every label covers about the same number of rows, which matters for skewed attributes "kmeans" centers of a 1-D k-means (deterministic, quantile-initialised): follows natural clusters and membership is "triangular" and "trapezoidal" (both Ruspini partitions, rows sum to 1) or "gaussian" (width chosen so neighbouring sets cross at degree 0.5). Default labels are low/high , low/medium/high , low/medium_low/medium_high/high , very_low/.../very_high , or L1..Ln . The resulting parameters are stored in fuzzy_lib.partitions[attribute]["params"] so you can reuse them with Fuzzification on new data. A constant attribute (not enough distinct values for n_labels peaks) raises a ValueError naming it. fuzzy_lib.AutoFuzzification(["age", "cholesterol"], n_labels=3, method="quantile") # -> ['age_low', 'age_medium', 'age_high', 'cholesterol_low', 'cholesterol_medium', 'cholesterol_high'] Feeding the fuzzy miners GetFuzzyTransactions(columns=None, min_degree=0.0) Returns one list of (item, degree) pairs per row -- the input format of FFIM.fuzzy_fpgrowth and of the fuzzy rule functions ( ARM.negative_rules , ARM.meta_rules ) -- using the columns added by Fuzzification / AutoFuzzification (or those in columns ) and skipping items whose degree is not greater than min_degree : from ARMxtend.FFIM import fuzzy_fpgrowth from ARMxtend.FIM.FARE import fuzzy_association_rules itemsets = fuzzy_fpgrowth(fuzzy_lib.GetFuzzyTransactions(), min_supp=0.1, num_alpha=10) rules = fuzzy_association_rules(itemsets, 10, metric="certainty_factor", min_threshold=0.5)

docs.text: Fuzzification(Atri, thresholds, FuzzyLabel, membership="triangular") Atri ( list[str] ): names of the numeric attributes to fuzzify. thresholds ( list[list] ): for each attribute, the parameters of its fuzzy sets, one per label: ascending peaks ( membership="triangular" ), (a, b, c, d) vertices ( "trapezoidal" ) or (center, sigma) pairs ( "gaussian" ). FuzzyLabel ( list[list[str]] ): for each attribute, the name of each fuzzy label (same length as its thresholds entry). membership ( str ): "triangular" (default), "trapezoidal" or "gaussian" -- see below. With the default membership="triangular" , this computes a triangular Ruspini partition : given n ascending peaks p_1 < ... < p_n (one per label), the two extreme labels are "shoulders" (full membership beyond their own peak) and the intermediate ones are triangles centered on their peak, so that the membership degrees of all n labels always sum to 1 for every row. It adds one new column <attribute>_<label> per label, with its membership degree, and returns the list of added column names. import pandas as pd from ARMxtend.preprocessing import FuzzyLib fuzzy_lib = FuzzyLib() fuzzy_lib.data = pd.DataFrame({"temperature": [15, 19, 22, 25, 28]}) added_columns = fuzzy_lib.Fuzzification(["temperature"], [[18, 22, 26]], [["cold", "comfort", "warm"]]) print(fuzzy_lib.data) # temperature temperature_cold temperature_comfort temperature_warm # 0 15 1.00 0.00 0.00 # 1 19 0.75 0.25 0.00 # 2 22 0.00 1.00 0.00 # 3 25 0.00 0.25 0.75 # 4 28 0.00 0.00 1.00 Each row's fuzzified columns for that attribute sum to 1: fuzzy_lib.data[added_columns].sum(axis=1) .
